title: Why a Surgeon Wrapped a Boy's Leg in Acid
topic: Why Joseph Lister sprayed carbolic acid over his patients during surgery

lines: A surgeon wrapped a boy's broken leg in acid-soaked towels.
It was 1865, and the bone had burst through the skin.
Normally, that meant cutting the leg off.
At his hospital, sixteen of thirty-five surgery patients died.
Wounds filled with pus. Gangrene ate living flesh.
Doctors blamed bad air. They didn't even wash their hands.
But Joseph Lister believed tiny germs were rotting the wounds.
Louis Pasteur had shown that germs make things decay.
And in Carlisle, a chemical called carbolic acid was killing the stink of sewage.
You see, it's like a cut you clean right away. It heals. Leave it dirty, and it swells.
So Lister set the bone and soaked clean towels in pure carbolic acid.
He covered the wound with tin foil and waited four days.
No infection. Just a little redness where the acid burned.
Six weeks later, the boy walked home.
After that, deaths fell to six in forty.
But the acid irritated skin so much that surgeons finally learned to keep germs out completely.

claims.claim: On August 12, 1865, Lister treated an eleven-year-old boy whose fractured tibia pierced the skin; amputation would ordinarily be the only solution.
Before antiseptic operations there were sixteen deaths in thirty-five surgical cases; afterwards six deaths in forty cases.
Hospital gangrene rots living tissue with remarkable rapidity; Lister saw pus in wounds.
Doctors blamed miasma ('bad air'); surgeons were not required to wash their hands.
Lister recognised that putrefaction in wounds is caused by germs, in connection to Pasteur's germ theory.
In Carlisle, officials experimented with carbolic acid to reduce the smell of sewage.

Lister set the bone, soaked clean cotton towels in undiluted carbolic acid, covered them with tin foil for four days, found no infection, only redness from mild burning; the boy walked home after about six weeks.
Skin irritation from continual exposure to phenol eventually led to aseptic (germ-free) techniques.
